content.title: About
content.content: Liqueur is an alcoholic beverage made by infusing, flavoring, and sweetening a base spirit with a variety of ingredients such as fruits, herbs, spices, nuts, and other aromatic compounds. Its alcohol by volume typically ranges from 15 % to 55 %.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest liqueurs were produced in ancient Egypt, where a honey‑wine infusion was used.
The word “liqueur” comes from the French “liqueur,” meaning “solution.”
Classic Italian amaro is a bitter herbal liqueur often served as a digestif.
In many countries liqueurs are classified as “spirit drinks with additives,” not as “dessert wines.”
Liqueurs are widely used in cooking, for sauces, desserts, and marinades.

items.title: Antioxidant components
items.content: Herbal and fruit extracts in liqueurs can provide polyphenols with antioxidant activity.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Bitter liqueurs (e.g., amaro) stimulate gastric secretions, supporting digestion.

items.title: Thermal effect
items.content: Moderate consumption of high‑proof liqueurs creates a warming sensation, sometimes used in traditional remedies for colds.

items.title: High alcohol content
items.content: Liqueurs can contain up to 55 % alcohol; excessive intake leads to intoxication and long‑term health issues.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some flavorings (e.g., nuts, shellfish) may trigger allergies.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol in liqueurs can amplify the effects of sedatives and antihypertensive drugs.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Most liqueurs are sweetened, which can be problematic for people with diabetes or weight concerns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Liqueur is typically served in small glasses (30–50 ml) as a digestif after meals, in cocktails, or as an aromatic addition to desserts. It can be drizzled over ice cream, mixed into sauces, or used in culinary recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep liqueur in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight. At temperatures above 20 °C the aroma may change over time, and opened bottles can undergo oxidative degradation.
